Super Fun 21: How This Blackjack Variant's Bonus Payouts Change the Math

Published November 3, 2026 · 10 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Super Fun 21 earns its cheerful name honestly — it's one of the few blackjack variants built almost entirely around giving the player extra ways to win, rather than extra ways for the house to claw money back. That's also exactly why it's worth understanding before you sit down: the game trades away the standard 3:2 blackjack payout for a smaller one, then tries to make up the difference with a pile of bonus rules most players have never seen on a felt. Whether that trade actually works in your favor depends on which of those rules you're playing with, and most players never bother to check.

What actually makes Super Fun 21 different

Super Fun 21 is usually dealt from one or two hand-held decks, though six-deck shoe versions exist at some properties, and the dealer hits a soft 17 across the board. On top of that standard shell, the game layers four signature rules: a player blackjack can never lose or push, even against a dealer blackjack; a regular blackjack pays even money instead of 3:2, except for one specific suited combination; a five-card hand totaling 21 pays double automatically; and a six-card hand that hasn't busted wins outright regardless of its total. Each one of those rules moves the math in a different direction, and understanding them individually is the only way to tell whether a specific table is actually a good deal.

Your blackjack always wins — even against the dealer's

In standard blackjack, if you draw a natural 21 and the dealer also draws one, the hand pushes and your bet comes back with no profit. Super Fun 21 removes that outcome entirely: a player blackjack is a guaranteed winner, full stop, even on the rare occasion the dealer also has one underneath. It's a small rule in terms of how often it actually comes up — two naturals in the same hand is a low-probability event — but it's a genuine, unambiguous giveback to the player with no catch attached, which is more than can be said for some of the game's other headline features.

Even money instead of 3:2, with one diamond-shaped exception

This is the rule that does the most damage, and the one a lot of players don't clock until they've already been paid. A standard blackjack that would pay $15 on a $10 bet at a 3:2 table pays only $10 at even money here — the same gap in value that makes a 6:5 table a bad deal, just reached by a different route. The one carve-out: a blackjack made specifically with the ace of diamonds and a diamond ten-value card pays 2 to 1 instead, which is a genuinely strong payout, but it only applies to that exact suited combination. Every non-diamond blackjack, which is the overwhelming majority of naturals you'll actually draw, settles at even money.

This single rule is why Super Fun 21 isn't automatically a better game than a well-chosen standard table. Our 6:5 payout breakdown walks through just how much a capped blackjack payout costs over time, and the even-money rule here sits in roughly that same neighborhood of lost value on every natural that isn't a diamond.

Automatic winners: 5-card 21s and 6-card hands

Here's where the game tries to pay you back. Any hand that reaches 21 using five or more cards pays 2 to 1 on the spot, regardless of how the dealer's hand turns out. Push the total further and the rule gets even more generous: a hand of six or more cards that totals 20 or less — one that hasn't busted — wins automatically at even money, again without needing to beat the dealer's total at all. Both bonuses have one important exception: neither applies to a hand you reached by doubling down, since the game's rules specifically exclude doubled hands from the instant-winner bonuses.

These rules reward exactly the kind of hand that feels nerve-wracking in standard blackjack — drawing card after card on a stiff total, hoping not to bust — and turn it into a bonus opportunity instead. They won't come up often enough to offset the even-money blackjack rule on their own, but they meaningfully soften it.

Worth remembering at the table: none of Super Fun 21's bonus payouts apply once you've doubled down. If you're holding a stiff hand and weighing a double, know that you're trading away the five-card and six-card bonus potential on that hand in exchange for the extra wager.

Doubling down, and the rescue option that limits the damage

Super Fun 21 is unusually permissive about when you can double: on any two or more cards, after hitting, and after splitting — including after splitting aces — with the catch that you only draw one card once you've doubled. That flexibility is paired with a genuine safety valve most blackjack variants don't offer: you can surrender half your bet on any hand totaling less than 21 even after you've doubled down, hit, or split, effectively letting you walk back a double that's gone badly wrong rather than riding it to a full loss. The one restriction is that surrender isn't available once the dealer has already turned up a blackjack. This combination — double almost anywhere, surrender almost anywhere, including out of a bad double — is one of the more player-friendly structural features of the game and worth using deliberately rather than ignoring.

Splitting rules

Pairs can be split up to three times, for a maximum of four hands from a single starting pair, and that split allowance explicitly includes aces — so unlike many standard blackjack tables that cap split aces at one card each with no resplitting, Super Fun 21 generally lets you resplit aces and even hit or double them like any other split hand. That's a genuine rule advantage over a lot of standard tables, though it's also a detail that varies by casino, so it's worth confirming at the specific table you're playing rather than assuming every property runs it the same way.

So does it actually beat standard blackjack?

There's no single answer, because it depends on which specific rule set and deck count a given casino is running — the same way a Strip blackjack table and a Downtown one can both say "blackjack" on the felt and carry meaningfully different house edges. What's consistent is the shape of the trade: Super Fun 21 gives up real value on the most common winning hand in the game (a plain blackjack) in exchange for a cluster of lower-frequency bonuses and player-friendly flexibility on doubling, splitting, and surrender. For a player who uses the double-down-rescue option and the liberal splitting rules correctly, that package can land closer to a standard 3:2 game than the even-money headline suggests. For a player who ignores those options and just plays stiff hands straight, the even-money blackjack rule is the one that actually shows up on every scorecard, and it's a real cost.

The practical move is the same one that applies to every blackjack variant with an unusual name: read the actual payout card at the table before buying in, don't assume the "fun" branding means the rules favor you by default, and specifically check whether that table still pays 3:2 on blackjack elsewhere in the house before deciding this version is the better seat.

Frequently asked questions

Does a player blackjack ever lose or push in Super Fun 21?

No. A player blackjack is a guaranteed winner under the game's rules, even in the rare case where the dealer also has a blackjack underneath — a hand that would simply push in standard blackjack.

Why does Super Fun 21 pay even money on blackjack instead of 3:2?

The even-money payout is how the game funds its other giveaways — the guaranteed player-blackjack rule, the automatic 5-card and 6-card bonuses, and the flexible doubling and surrender rules. The one exception is a blackjack made with the ace of diamonds and a diamond ten-value card, which pays 2 to 1.

What happens if I double down and then draw a 5-card 21?

You don't get the bonus. The automatic 2:1 payout for a 5-card 21, and the automatic win for a 6-or-more-card hand of 20 or less, both explicitly exclude hands reached by doubling down.

Can I surrender after I've already doubled my bet?

Generally yes — this is sometimes called a "double down rescue." You can surrender one of the two bets on a doubled hand totaling less than 21, which caps your loss at the original wager instead of the full doubled amount. Surrender isn't available once the dealer has already shown a blackjack.

Can I resplit aces in Super Fun 21?

At most tables, yes — pairs including aces can generally be split up to three times for a maximum of four hands, and split aces can typically be hit or doubled like any other split hand. Rules can vary by casino, so it's worth confirming at the specific table.
